title: Policy and concentrated supply set to drive rare-earth magnet prices
gist: Oxford Economics has added price forecasts for the four magnet rare earths (neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium) and expects gradual but uneven price growth through 2035, with the heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium most exposed to concentrated supply and export controls. China's chokepoint is midstream rather than at the mine — 60% of magnet rare-earth mining but 91% of refining and 94% of permanent-magnet output in 2024 — and western policy support is building a parallel, higher-cost market rather than displacing the Chinese core.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has added price forecasts for neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium — the four rare earth elements central to high-performance permanent magnets — to its Global Commodities Service, signalling that magnet rare earths are now a mainstream forecastable commodity class rather than a niche.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Formal sell-side/consultancy price curves for magnet rare earths give procurement and mining equity investors a benchmark to trade contract pricing and miner NPVs against.
insights.quote: We have added forecasts for neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium—the four rare earth elements central to high-performance permanent magnets
insights.locator: We have added forecasts for neodymium

insights.claim: Prices for the four magnet rare earths are forecast to grow gradually but not uniformly through 2035, implying dispersion across the complex rather than a single beta trade on 'rare earths'.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The trade is relative-value within the rare-earth basket — long the tightest heavy elements versus the deeper light ones — not a blanket long on the sector.
insights.quote: Our forecasts point to gradual, but not uniform, price growth through 2035.
insights.locator: Our forecasts point to gradual, but not uniform

insights.claim: Demand for magnet rare earths is underpinned by a broad and structurally growing end-market set — electric vehicles, wind turbines, industrial motors, robotics, data centres and defence — so the demand base is diversified beyond the EV cycle alone.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: An EV sales slowdown alone should not break the rare-earth demand story; robotics, data centres and defence procurement provide offsetting bids.
insights.quote: Demand is supported by electric vehicles, wind turbines, industrial motors, robotics, data centres, and defence applications.
insights.locator: Demand is supported by electric vehicles

insights.claim: Neodymium and praseodymium trade in larger light-rare-earth markets, while dysprosium and terbium are smaller heavy-rare-earth markets with more concentrated supply and greater exposure to export controls — making the heavies structurally more price-volatile and politically exposed.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Position size and hedge the heavy rare earths differently from the lights: dysprosium and terbium carry the export-control tail risk and the thinner order books.
insights.quote: Neodymium and praseodymium are larger light-rare-earth markets, while dysprosium and terbium are smaller heavy-rare-earth markets with more concentrated supply and greater exposure to export controls.
insights.locator: Neodymium and praseodymium are larger light-rare-earth markets

themes.theme: Thrifting and recycling as partial, slow buffers

insights.claim: Magnet manufacturers have already cut heavy-rare-earth intensity through improved motor design and greater material efficiency, so demand-side innovation should temper rather than eliminate upward price pressure on dysprosium and terbium.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate magnet demand linearly from EV or motor unit growth — per-unit heavy rare-earth content is falling, capping the volume upside for miners.
insights.quote: Demand-side innovation should temper, rather than eliminate, these pressures.

insights.claim: Recycling of end-of-life electric-vehicle motors, wind turbines and electronics will become a materially larger source of magnet rare-earth supply as installed fleets age, creating a secondary-supply channel that did not previously exist at scale.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Watch rare-earth recyclers and scrap-stream aggregators as a late-cycle competitor to primary miners' long-dated volume assumptions.
insights.quote: Recycling will also become more important as larger volumes of electric-vehicle motors, wind turbines, and electronics reach end of life.
insights.locator: Recycling will also become more important

insights.claim: Because thrifting and recycling require investment, technical qualification and reliable scrap streams, they constrain long-run demand per unit of equipment but offer limited protection against a sudden near-term supply shock.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The substitution story is a long-duration cap on prices, not a near-term hedge — spike risk from an export-control event remains fully live.
insights.quote: These changes constrain long-run demand per unit of equipment, but they require investment, technical qualification, and reliable scrap streams, so they provide limited protection against a sudden near-term supply shock.
insights.locator: These changes constrain long-run demand per unit

themes.theme: China's midstream chokepoint and the two-tier western market

insights.claim: China accounted for 60% of magnet rare-earth mining but 91% of refining and 94% of permanent-magnet production in 2024, meaning its leverage sits in the midstream and magnet-making steps rather than at the mine.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: New non-Chinese mines do not break the dependency; separation, refining and magnet-making capacity is the binding constraint and where policy money and equity upside should concentrate.
insights.quote: China’s position is strongest beyond the mine: it accounted for 60% of magnet rare-earth mining but 91% of refining and 94% of permanent-magnet production in 2024.
insights.locator: China’s position is strongest beyond the mine

insights.claim: Western policy support for alternative rare-earth capacity is creating a higher-cost western market that sits alongside — rather than displaces — the Chinese core, implying a persistent two-tier price structure for magnet rare earths.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Western rare-earth projects need price floors, offtakes or subsidies to be viable; underwrite them on policy-supported premium pricing, not on the Chinese benchmark.
insights.quote: Policy support can build alternative capacity, but it is also creating a higher-cost western market alongside the Chinese core.
insights.locator: Policy support can build alternative capacity
